questions.def: "Although" introduces a contrast, forming an adverbial clause of concession.
questions.question: ___ he studies hard, he still finds exams difficult.

questions.def: "As soon as" indicates immediate succession, acting as a time adverbial.
questions.question: I will call you ___ I arrive at the hotel.

questions.def: "Despite" doesn't take "of"; it's followed directly by the noun.
questions.question: Despite of the rain, we went for a walk.

questions.def: "Having finished" is a perfect participle clause showing completed action.
questions.question: ___ the project, he went home.

questions.def: "So as" expresses purpose; an adverbial clause of purpose.
questions.question: She spoke quietly ___ not to wake the baby.

questions.def: "Despite" is followed by a gerund phrase, showing concession.
questions.question: ___ being tired, he stayed up late to finish the report.

questions.def: After "unless", use the present simple, not "will".
questions.question: He will go unless it will rain.

questions.def: "Knowing" introduces a reason as a participle clause.
questions.question: ___ the risks, he accepted the challenge.

questions.def: "Because of" is followed by a noun phrase, showing cause.
questions.question: ___ the fire, the building was evacuated quickly.

questions.def: "However" introduces a contrast, often with an adjective/adverb.
questions.question: ___ hard he tried, he couldn't open the door.

questions.def: When using "while" with a reduced clause, use present participle.
questions.question: While walked in the park, I saw an old friend.

questions.def: "Invited" acts as a reduced passive adverbial clause.
questions.question: ___ to the party, she felt very happy.

questions.def: "Regardless of" means "without considering" and precedes a noun.
questions.question: ___ the cost, the project was approved.

questions.def: "As if" introduces a hypothetical situation, often with subjunctive.
questions.question: He behaved ___ he were the boss.

questions.def: It should be "Due to the traffic", not "Due of the traffic".
questions.question: Due of the traffic, we were late.

questions.def: "Living" introduces a circumstance as a participle clause.
questions.question: ___ in London, he learned a lot.

questions.def: "If" introduces a condition; a conditional adverbial clause.
questions.question: ___ you need help, just ask.

questions.def: "So that" introduces a purpose, often followed by "can/could".
questions.question: He ran ___ he could catch the train.

questions.def: In "even if" clauses, use present simple, not "will".
questions.question: Even if the price will rise, we will buy it.

questions.def: "Seeing" is a present participle clause indicating cause.
questions.question: ___ the opportunity, he seized it.

questions.def: "Despite the fact that" shows concession.
questions.question: ___ the fact that it was raining, they enjoyed the picnic.

questions.def: "When" indicates a point in time; an adverbial clause of time.
questions.question: I will give you a call ___ I get home.

questions.def: "In spite of" is followed by a noun/gerund, not a clause.
questions.question: In spite of he was tired, he kept working.

questions.def: "Having understood" shows a completed action influencing the main clause.
questions.question: ___ the instructions, he began the task.

questions.def: "Even though" indicates a strong contrast; an adverbial clause.
questions.question: ___ he had a fever, he still went to work.

questions.def: "In order to" expresses purpose and is followed by the base form.
questions.question: She exercises regularly ___ stay healthy.

questions.def: "Unless" already has a negative meaning; don't use "won't".
questions.question: Unless you won't study, you will fail.

questions.def: "Not knowing" is a negative participle clause showing reason.
questions.question: ___ what to do, he asked for help.

questions.def: "Until" indicates a time limit; an adverbial clause of time.
questions.question: ___ I finish this report, I can't go home.

questions.def: "So that" introduces a purpose, often followed by "can/could".
questions.question: He worked ___ he could finish the project on time.
